clue.text: Place at Brighton for retired cricketers

blocks.note: first meaning: the Royal ..., the Prince Regent's oriental palace in the seaside town of Brighton
second meaning: the building at a cricket ground where a batsman goes when he retires from the crease

explanation.surface: A seaside retirement home for old cricket players.
explanation.walkthrough: Retired cricketers sounds like elderly players, but in cricket a batsman who retires simply walks off the field to the clubhouse.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both the famous Regency palace in Brighton and the clubhouse building beside a cricket field.

clue.text: Girl used in 11 across

blocks.note: first meaning: a female first name
second meaning: a red precious stone, the kind of thing a jeweller cuts

explanation.walkthrough: 11 across is GEM CUTTING, whose clue itself contains a cut-down version of this stone.
explanation.definitionFit: It is both a common female forename and a red gemstone that lapidaries shape and polish.

clue.text: Put up horse in frisky ride

indicators.note: a frisky animal jumps about, so the letters of the word beside it are tossed into a new order
one element is placed inside another, the outer word wrapping it

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
GG, short for gee-gee, is a childish word for a horse

explanation.surface: Someone sets a horse up for a lively outing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put up' looks like stabling a horse, but here it means fixed in advance, as in a put-up job.
explanation.definitionFit: A put-up job is a fraud arranged beforehand, which is exactly what a fixed or crooked contest is.

clue.text: Thomas could first muster up courage for the fight

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the neighbouring word is kept
to muster is to gather troops and form them up in a new order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
the initial letter of this word

explanation.surface: Doubting Thomas might summon the nerve to go into battle.
explanation.walkthrough: Having the stomach for something means having the nerve or appetite to face it.
explanation.definitionFit: Stomach in the idiomatic sense is the nerve or willingness needed to face a difficult or unpleasant struggle.

clue.text: Do they weigh on the conscience?

definitions.text: Do they weigh on the conscience?

blocks.clueFragment: Do they weigh on the conscience?
blocks.note: surface reading: worries that press heavily on a guilty mind
setter's reading: these are also small apothecaries' weights, so they literally weigh things, as well as being moral hesitations

explanation.walkthrough: The word is both an old apothecaries' unit of weight, a twentieth of an ounce, and a moral qualm.
explanation.definitionFit: Moral hesitations that trouble a person's sense of right are the qualms meant, punning on a tiny old pharmacist's weight.

clue.text: Where an archbishop keeps his books?

definitions.text: Where an archbishop keeps his books?

blocks.clueFragment: Where an archbishop keeps his books?
blocks.note: surface reading: an archbishop's library or study
setter's reading: the senior Church of England archbishop takes his title from a city whose name is also a small stand for books and music

explanation.walkthrough: The word is a Kent cathedral city, seat of the senior English archbishop, and also a low stand with partitions for holding books or sheet music.
explanation.definitionFit: A piece of furniture with slotted divisions for storing papers shares its name with the archbishop's own see.

clue.text: Stone I cut from hewn granite

indicators.note: something cut from a larger whole is removed from it
rock that is hewn is chopped up and reshaped, so the remaining letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
this letter is the piece removed

explanation.surface: A mason cuts a stone out of a block of rough-hewn rock.
explanation.definitionFit: The deep red silicate mineral is a semi-precious gem, so it is a kind of precious stone.

clue.text: Someone who never wears out

blocks.note: surface reading: a tireless person who never becomes exhausted
setter's reading: a person who puts on no clothes when outside

explanation.walkthrough: 'Wears out' looks like the phrasal verb for tiring, but split it: this person never wears anything when out.
explanation.definitionFit: A nudist goes about unclothed by choice, so in public they wear nothing at all.

clue.text: They could be involved in a crash

definitions.text: They could be involved in a crash

indicators.note: involved means tangled or twisted up, so the letters are mixed into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A warning that certain vehicles might end up in a collision.
explanation.walkthrough: A chara is short for charabanc, an old open motor coach for outings; the whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Old motor coaches are vehicles, and vehicles are exactly the things that can end up in a road collision.

clue.text: Girl likely to be heartless

indicators.note: without a heart means the middle letters of the word are taken away

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A young woman who will probably turn out to be cruel.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a common female forename, taken from the flower.

clue.text: Jeweller's work could make Cornelia rub, etc

blocks.note: surface reading: some task that would make a woman called Cornelia start rubbing
setter's reading: chop the last letter off precious stone names, cornelian and the red one, and you get these words

explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer literally as trimming jewels: cornelian loses its N, the red stone loses its Y, and so on.
explanation.definitionFit: A lapidary's craft is shaping and faceting precious stones, which is exactly what a jeweller's cutting trade involves.

clue.text: Namely, a hollow red mask

indicators.note: something hollow has its inside emptied, so only the outside letters of the word stay

blocks.note: viz is the abbreviation meaning namely
taken as written
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: Specifically, an empty crimson face covering.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an archaic word for a visor or face covering worn to disguise the wearer.

clue.text: A great egg's smashed - stuff for the mixer

indicators.note: a smashed egg is broken apart, so these letters are broken up and rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A big egg broken into a cake mix in the kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: The mixer sounds like a kitchen food mixer, but it is a concrete mixer.
explanation.definitionFit: Sand, gravel and crushed stone are the materials poured into a cement mixer to make concrete.

clue.text: Speed created when centre of star drops out

indicators.note: points to the middle letter of the word that follows
a letter that drops out leaves the word and is lost

blocks.note: a famous person, a star of screen or sport

explanation.surface: A star's middle collapses and things happen fast.
explanation.walkthrough: Star suggests astronomy, but it is a famous person, and its middle letter, the fifth of nine, is removed.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a formal word for swiftness or rapidity of movement.

clue.text: Example of where the stick is thickest

definitions.text: Example of where the stick is thickest

blocks.note: surface reading: the fattest part of a stick or club
setter's reading: these eight letters rearranged spell the clue's last word, so the phrase is an instance of a wordplay device

explanation.walkthrough: The clue is self-referential: 'the stick' and 'thickest' share the same eight letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A word or phrase formed by rearranging the letters of another is the device this clue demonstrates.

clue.text: Diamonds once formed from very hard sulphur

blocks.note: an adjective meaning unyielding, from a legendary hard stone
S is the chemical symbol for sulphur

explanation.surface: Gems made long ago from tough sulphur deposits.
explanation.definitionFit: The word was an old name for diamond or any impenetrably hard stone, hence 'once' for its archaic use.

clue.text: Kind of English issuing from big mouth!

blocks.note: first meaning: the accent of south-east England around the Thames, a blend of Cockney and standard speech
second meaning: the wide tidal mouth of a river

explanation.surface: A particular accent pouring out of a loudmouth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big mouth' suggests a boastful talker, but it is a river's mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: The name of the Thames-side accent comes from the tidal river inlet, the broad opening where a river meets the sea.

clue.text: What the highest jumper does at the back?

blocks.note: first meaning, read as two words: a horse that leaps up highest on its hind legs is the one that rears most
second meaning: furthest to the rear

explanation.walkthrough: The first reading splits the word: a jumping horse rears, and the highest one does so most.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is the superlative of rear, meaning the very last in position, furthest behind.

clue.text: Bird crossing the road?

blocks.note: first meaning: a large water bird with a throat pouch
second meaning: in Britain a pedestrian crossing controlled by push-button traffic lights

explanation.surface: Why did the bird cross the road?
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a pelican crossing is a pedestrian crossing with lights the walker operates.
explanation.definitionFit: The pouched seabird gives its name to a light-controlled British street crossing for walkers.

clue.text: Order cream tea? That's steep!

indicators.note: to order things is to arrange them, so the letters are put into a new sequence

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A café customer orders scones and is shocked by the price.
explanation.walkthrough: A cream tea is a British afternoon snack of tea with scones, jam and clotted cream; 'steep' looks like an expensive price, but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To soak food in liquid until it softens is to steep it, as fruit in alcohol.

clue.text: Leaders of army coup go free

indicators.note: leaders are the ones at the front, so the opening letters of the next words are taken

blocks.note: the initial letters of these two words
to quit is to leave or go

explanation.surface: The generals behind a military takeover are let off.
explanation.definitionFit: To free in the legal sense is to clear a defendant of a charge and release them.

clue.text: Amateur performer of 22 down?

definitions.note: read as two words, a man of lays

blocks.note: first meaning: a non-professional, someone without expert training
second meaning, split in two: 22 down is art-songs, and a lay is a song

explanation.walkthrough: 22 down is LIEDER, German art-songs; a lay is an old word for a song or ballad.
explanation.definitionFit: A non-specialist outside a profession is an amateur in that field, someone untrained in its expertise.

clue.text: I*d reel out art-songs

indicators.note: out here means awry or disordered, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, ignoring the asterisk

explanation.surface: A singer says they would rattle off a string of concert songs.
explanation.definitionFit: German romantic songs for solo voice and piano, such as Schubert's, are known in English by their German plural name.

clue.text: Water with jolly blue colour

blocks.note: aqua is the Latin word for water
a jolly is old naval slang for a Royal Marine

explanation.surface: Cheerful water of a bright blue hue.
explanation.walkthrough: Jolly looks like an adjective, but in British naval slang it is a noun for a Royal Marine.
explanation.definitionFit: The pale greenish-blue shade takes its name from the sea-coloured gemstone, beryl of that tint.

clue.text: Does the dismissed athlete take it running?

definitions.text: Does the dismissed athlete take it running?

blocks.clueFragment: Does the dismissed athlete take it running?
blocks.note: surface reading: does a sacked sportsman accept the news on the move?
setter's reading: someone told to go away is told to take a running one, an idiom of dismissal, and for an athlete it is also an event

explanation.walkthrough: 'Go and take a running jump' is a rude British way of telling someone to go away, so a dismissed person takes one.
explanation.definitionFit: A leap made after a run-up is an athletic event, and taking one is the idiom for being sent packing.

clue.text: The Augustus who painted gents?

blocks.note: first meaning: the surname of the Welsh portrait painter Augustus, 1878 to 1961
second meaning: an informal word for a lavatory; the gents is a British name for a men's public toilet

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as if the artist painted portraits of gentlemen, but 'gents' is a separate meaning: a men's toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname of a famous Welsh painter is also American slang for a toilet, which the British call the gents.

clue.text: Turn off! I'd come back green

indicators.note: to come back is to return, so the word is read from right to left

blocks.note: the contraction without its apostrophe
vert is the heraldic term for green

explanation.surface: Someone snaps that they will go back to being an environmentalist.
explanation.definitionFit: To turn off a road is to change course, which means to redirect or deflect traffic onto another route.

clue.text: May the small stone change colour?

indicators.note: to change is to alter, so the letters are put into a different order

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
st is the short form of stone, the British unit of weight

explanation.surface: A wish that a little pebble might alter its hue.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites the stone itself as answer, but the definition is the last word: the name is also a purple shade.
explanation.definitionFit: The violet quartz gives its name to a purple shade, so the word is used as a colour.
